newsitem.title: UK: Funds reaped $400 mln profits in 93-95 coffee boom.
newsitem.headline: Funds reaped $400 mln profits in 93-95 coffee boom.

text.p: The last major coffee boom in 1993 to 1995 netted over $400 million in profits for speculators particularly the funds, a study by the University of London revealed.

"Our central estimates show large speculators as having made a second and third quarter 1994 profit on CSCE (the New York arabica coffee futures) of over $600 million and a profit of over $400 million over the entire 1994-95 period," said the study.
A copy of the report was released this week.

"Since small speculators also made money, this implies large losses to hedgers - of the order of $900 million in the second and third quarters of 1994 and $550 million over the entire period," it said.
The study by economics lecturer Christpher Gilbert and a PhD student Celso Brunetti centred on the aspect of speculation, hedging and volatility in the market between 1993 and 1996.
The rise in coffee prices in 1993-95 took place against a background of a general recovery in non-oil primary commodity prices but coffee showed the greatest proportionate gain, the study said.
There was a sharp jump in price volatility on the coffee market in 1994, whereas commodity volatility in general did not change substantially over the period, it said.
"Clearly, the hedge funds and other financial investors who put money into coffee in the initial months of 1994 did very well out of their investments," the study added.

It said it was difficult to calculate precisely how well, both because it did not know the scale of the funds investments on the London coffee market and because it must guess at the trading strategies they adopted.
What moved the funds into coffee?
Gilbert and Brunetti said there were three distinct episodes in the pattern of coffee market speculation over 1993-995.
Speculation in the summer of 1993 was motivated by coffee retention decisions announced by producers in September.

The large speculative build-up which started in February 1994 was, by contrast, the result of the decisions by hedge fund and other investment managers to diversify out of bond and equity markets into a number of "non-traditional" investments including commodities.
So speculators were fortunate to have accumulated large long positions when the Brazilian frosts hit the market in June and July 1994.
"They could have not anticipated what was a very unusual period of weather, and were long in coffee primarily for portfolio diversification reasons...", the researchers said.
The third and last phase was during 1995 and the first part of 1996, and again motivated by specific coffee market factors.
Looking ahead, the report concluded: "It is possible, perhaps even likely, that the coffee market will now be more placid than it has been over the period since 1993."
